title: Healthcare & Medical Privacy Privacy Hardening Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect your medical data, secure health apps, ensure HIPAA compliance, and safeguard reproductive health information.
intro: Your medical information is among your most sensitive personal data. From health apps selling your data to HIPAA gaps in telehealth services, protecting your healthcare privacy requires proactive steps. This checklist helps secure your medical data across all platforms.

items.task: Audit all health apps on your devices
items.why: Many health apps aren't covered by HIPAA and may sell your data to third parties or advertisers.
items.howTo: List all health, fitness, period tracking, and medical apps. Check each app's privacy policy for data sharing practices. Delete apps that sell data or lack clear privacy protections.

items.task: Switch to privacy-focused period tracking apps
items.why: Period data can reveal pregnancy status and reproductive choices, which could be legally compromised in certain jurisdictions.
items.howTo: Use apps like Euki or Drip that store data locally on your device. Avoid cloud-synced apps that share data with third parties. Consider offline tracking methods.

items.task: Review fitness tracker data sharing settings
items.why: Fitness trackers collect health metrics that can reveal medical conditions and are often shared with insurance companies.
items.howTo: Access your fitness app settings and disable data sharing with third parties. Turn off health insights sharing and advertising personalization. Limit data syncing to essential features only.

items.why: Health apps often request excessive permissions that allow access to contacts, location, and other sensitive data.
items.howTo: Go to phone settings > Apps > [Health App] > Permissions. Disable location, contacts, camera, and microphone access unless absolutely necessary for core functionality.

items.task: Secure mental health and therapy apps
items.why: Mental health data is highly sensitive and many apps lack proper encryption or share data with analytics companies.
items.howTo: Choose apps that offer end-to-end encryption. Verify the app doesn't share data with Facebook, Google Analytics, or advertising networks. Read recent privacy audits if available.

items.why: Symptom data can reveal medical conditions and treatment effectiveness, valuable to data brokers and insurance companies.
items.howTo: Use encrypted note-taking apps or offline tracking methods instead of specialized symptom apps. If using apps, choose ones with local data storage and no cloud syncing.

items.why: Telehealth sessions can be intercepted on unsecured networks, and your ISP can track medical website visits.
items.howTo: Connect to a reputable VPN before telehealth appointments. Use Incognito Browser for accessing patient portals to prevent tracking cookies and browsing history storage.

items.why: Not all video platforms used by healthcare providers meet HIPAA security standards for medical consultations.
items.howTo: Ask your provider which platform they use and if it's HIPAA-compliant. Prefer providers using dedicated medical platforms over generic video calling services.

items.why: Patient portals contain comprehensive medical records that are valuable targets for hackers and identity thieves.
items.howTo: Enable two-factor authentication on all patient portals. Use unique, strong passwords. Always log out completely after use. Clear browser data after accessing portals.

items.why: Prescription data reveals medical conditions and can be used for targeted advertising or insurance discrimination.
items.howTo: Use pharmacy websites that don't share data with advertising networks. Opt out of marketing communications. Use private browsing mode when ordering prescriptions online.

items.why: Medical emails and messages often contain sensitive health information that can be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized parties.
items.howTo: Use encrypted email providers for medical communications. Never discuss sensitive medical details in unsecured messages. Prefer secure patient portal messaging over regular email.

items.why: Understanding your rights helps you control how your medical information is used and shared by healthcare providers.
items.howTo: Request a copy of your healthcare provider's Notice of Privacy Practices. Learn about your rights to access, amend, and restrict use of your health information.

items.task: Request and review your medical records
items.why: Regular review helps you identify unauthorized access and ensures accuracy of your medical information.
items.howTo: Submit written requests for your medical records from all providers. Review for accuracy and unauthorized access. Request corrections for any errors you find.

items.why: Healthcare providers often share patient information with pharmaceutical companies and marketing firms for promotional purposes.
items.howTo: Submit written requests to opt out of marketing communications with all healthcare providers. Specify you want to restrict use of your information for marketing purposes.

items.why: Insurance companies collect extensive health data and may share it with employers, data brokers, or other third parties.
items.howTo: Review your insurance privacy policy and opt out of data sharing where possible. Request information about what data is collected and how it's used.

items.why: Healthcare organizations experience frequent data breaches, exposing patient information to identity thieves and fraudsters.
items.howTo: Set up Google Alerts for your healthcare providers + 'data breach'. Check HHS breach report database quarterly. Monitor credit reports for signs of medical identity theft.

items.why: Medical research participation can lead to ongoing data collection and sharing that extends beyond the original study.
items.howTo: Read all research consent forms carefully. Ask about data retention periods and sharing practices. Request to opt out of future contact or data use when possible.

items.task: Opt out of medical data brokers
items.why: Data brokers collect and sell medical information from various sources, creating detailed health profiles used by marketers and insurers.
items.howTo: Identify major medical data brokers like LexisNexis, Experian Health, and Epsilon. Submit opt-out requests to each. Use data broker removal services for comprehensive coverage.

items.task: Limit pharmacy loyalty program data sharing
items.why: Pharmacy loyalty programs track prescription purchases and may share this data with manufacturers and advertisers.
items.howTo: Review loyalty program privacy policies and opt out of data sharing. Consider paying without loyalty programs for sensitive prescriptions. Use cash for maximum privacy.

items.why: Medical websites often use tracking pixels that share your health interests and concerns with advertising networks.
items.howTo: Use Incognito Browser when researching health conditions to prevent tracking. Install privacy-focused browser extensions that block medical website trackers and pixels.

items.why: Social media platforms analyze health-related posts and searches to build advertising profiles and may share data with third parties.
items.howTo: Avoid posting about health conditions on social media. Use private browsing for health-related searches. Adjust ad preferences to limit health-based targeting.

items.why: Location data can reveal visits to medical facilities, pharmacies, and specialists, creating detailed health profiles.
items.howTo: Turn off location services when visiting medical facilities. Use GPS spoofing apps if necessary. Park away from sensitive medical locations when possible.

pro_tips: Create a separate, encrypted email account specifically for medical communications to isolate health data from your main email.
Use cash payments for sensitive medical services and prescriptions to avoid creating digital payment trails that can be tracked.
Regular security audits of your health apps every 3 months - privacy policies change frequently and new data sharing practices are often introduced.
Consider using a dedicated phone number for medical appointments and services to limit cross-referencing of your health data with other personal information.
Keep offline backups of important medical records in case you need to delete digital copies for privacy reasons - use encrypted storage devices.
